newsitem.title: CROATIA: US ship delivers $100 million of arms for Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: US ship delivers $100 million of arms for Bosnia.

text.p: An American ship on Thursday began unloading a $100 million arms shipment to Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation long delayed by Washington's demand a Sarajevo official with ties to Iran be sacked.

In a ceremony aboard the American Condor, the U.S. envoy overseeing the military aid programme, James Pardew, said the heavy weapons being handed to the Federation forces gave them what "they needed for adequate defence".

The delivery marks the start of the controversial U.S.-led "Train and Equip" programme aimed at making allied Moslems and Croats a military match for the Bosnian Serbs whom they fought in the former Yugoslav republic's 43-month war.
"The U.S.S. American Condor contains 45 tanks and 80 armoured personnel carriers to help remove that disadvantage," Pardew said.
"The ship also contains over 5,000 pieces of communication gear, 15 utility helicopters, 45,000 rifles, ammunition and other equipment."

The American Condor first docked in Ploce weeks ago but set sail again to idle in the Adriatic until the Sarajevo government fulfilled a U.S. demand for the removal of Deputy Minister Hasan Cengic who they said was too closely tied to Iran.
Cengic's dismissal was finally confirmed on Tuesday.
The Federation's Vice President, Ejup Ganic, said the shipment provided the foundations for building stability in Bosnia.

"This is a historic day for the federation. We are building the Federation from the inside," he said. Disputes between Moslems and Croats, who fought a vicious war in 1993 and are now tied politically, had also delayed the arms delivery.
Another ship carying arms from the United Arab Emirates was also being off-loaded in Ploce, while an Egyptian shipment of artillery and air defence weapons was expected in the Croatian port soon.
European allies of the United States refused to participate in the programme, arguing that it was folly to pour more weapons into Bosnia barely a year after the war ended.
